On 2 and 3 applications come before people: in a crowded call a playing application still gets a fader. A dark slot shows the last pool of its chain (people on 2 and 3).

items.title: U4: people only in a call

Matters when call means less than "someone is in the voice chat", e.g. sitting in a Mumble lobby all evening with call toggled by a button. Slots that should never show people say apps: auto, also the implicit one at the end of a stack that can run out, takes people.

items.text: No entry, or auto: people from the right, applications from the left, on every slot that shows auto, as before.

items.title: Errors and notes of check-config
items.text:
Where Message [people] people: the section is [pool.people] now; the people sit on the slots whose stack names people or auto in_auto channel.voip: in_auto is in_pool now hold, exclude in [pool.auto] pool.auto: hold: an option of [pool.apps] now from, order, channels in [pool.auto] pool.auto: from: auto fills from the sides of [pool.apps] and [pool.people] (and the like) hold, exclude, channels in [pool.people] pool.people: hold: people stay absent_after seconds after they left (and the like) channels, order in [pool.apps] pool.apps: order: an option of [pool.people] (and the like) from pool.people.from: Input should be 'left' or 'right' a channel or state named apps, people or auto channel.apps: apps is a built-in pool a place of people slots.6[0]: rec is no option of a place for people (...) a pool of channels below a built-in one slots.2[1]: media below auto: a pool of channels goes above the pools auto, apps and people

check-config prints notes after the table: a channel right below a pool without a condition never shows (a pool hands down only to pools and -), and people: no slot shows people or auto, ... when the file has a person channel or [pool.people] options and no slot can show people.

items.title: The GUI
items.text:
• Slots: Shows offers apps, people and auto with the channels. The dot is on the candidate that fills the slot (on people while a person sits there). A pool without a condition reads when app without a slot → apps (an outlined chip) (tooltip: what a member needs, e.g. an application that plays and has no slot yet; revised 2026-11-18, it read left over → apps below another pool). A tiny LCD after each candidate has the color of its strip. The inspector says what a pool hands out and from where (Pool people: the people of the voice chat ..., from the right.), with the place options of its strips: those of an application for apps and auto, of a person for people, of a channel for a pool of channels.
  • Simulate: two counts next to the states, people in the call and applications that play; the device shows their names. apps fill and people fill are what-ifs where the stacks name them.
  • Grid: apps and people are dimensions where a stack names them (full: as many as slots), e.g. a row call, people fill.
  • Channels: the built-in pools [pool.apps], [pool.people] and [pool.auto] below the channels, each with its options and the look of its strips.
  • why: xtouch-daemon why people lists who sits where and who waits; a slot's why says people: none left for this slot when it was handed down.

items.title: Built
items.text:
Part Where Pools, options, errors, chain check slots/model.py (AppsConfig, PeopleConfig, AutoConfig, PoolConfig, _parse_pools(), _check_chains(), place_options()) Presence, members slots/inputs.py (pool_present(), people_of(), excluded()) Chains, hand-down, contest slots/resolver.py (_chain(), _of_channels(), _contest(), _fill_order()) Simulate, Grid, notes slots/outcomes.py (simulate() with counts, dimensions(), notes()), cli/configuration.py Strips of places config/slots.py, runtime/binder.py (people take the look of their place) GUI gui/domain/slot_stacks.py, gui/domain/simulate.py, gui/domain/channels.py, gui/qt/pages/slots.py, gui/qt/pages/channels.py

Tests are Markus's call; the existing ones that describe the old rules fail as expected (in_auto, [people], hold of [pool.auto], waiting["auto"], a pool of channels that was dark and now hands down).

items.title: Not chosen
items.text:
• People only as a pool, pools never fall through: slots meant for people are dark outside a call (the live test rejected that).
  • auto alone with options in [people] (from, slots, when, alone): a second language next to the stacks.
  • A preference per auto place (people = "first"): the same as stacks, hidden in an option.
  • A list of slots for people ([people] slots = [6, 5, 4]): a second place to edit when a slot moves.
  • A real block, or "first candidate first" for applications too: see Not a block.
  • +2 or paging when more people than slots: they wait; the why line and the live view say who.

items.title: Design: presets
items.text:
Status: implemented as described here; how to use it is in Presets.

The idea: common groups of applications (every browser, every voice chat, every game started from Steam) get a name, so nobody has to look up what each application calls its streams and processes. match = ["@browsers"] instead of match = ["brave", "firefox", "chromium", ...].

items.title: Where applications are matched by name
items.text:
Where Matched against Kind match of apps strips the application name (application.name) and binary (application.process.binary) of each stream streams apps of layouts the same streams behavior.ignore (what auto strips never take) the same streams processes of layouts the names of the processes (comm, and the file name of the program) processes "runs" of an apps strip with launch the processes, with the match entries processes the program of launch (all strips, also voip) the processes, the file name of the program exactly none: a command, not a list of names person of voip strips, [aliases] names of people, exact names of applications none

Presets go where the user writes a list of parts of names: the first four rows. The fifth follows from match.

items.title: How a preset is written
items.text:
• @name in the list, next to plain names: match = ["@voip", "my-voice-app"]. An @ never starts the name of an application or process in practice, and TOML needs no quoting beyond the string. A separate option (match_presets = [...]) was the alternative; one list is shorter and works the same in every list.
  • Names are lower case with hyphens: @steam-games.

items.title: What a preset stands for
items.text:
presets.py holds the table: each Preset has a description, the names for lists of streams (streams) and for lists of processes (processes), either of which may be None (not for that kind of list), and a note for the docs.

  • The names are matched like the user's: as parts of the name, ignoring case. A preset is nothing but a list of names, so it can't do anything the user could not write, and list-apps and check-config explain it in the same terms. Exact matching or regular expressions would be a second matching mode for little gain.
  • A preset stands for different names in each kind of list. Streams and processes are named differently: a Proton game plays as Planet Crafter.exe (binary wine64-preloader), but its processes are Wine's, and .exe in a list of processes matches Wine's helpers (explorer.exe, services.exe) and Proton's steam.exe. Steam starts every game through its reaper, which is the reliable process, and has no stream.
  • Errors at validation. An unknown preset lists the known ones. A preset in a list it has no names for says where it can be used. Both are pydantic errors of the option, so check-config and the GUI show them at their place (strip[2].match: ...).

items.title: Expanded when the configuration is validated
items.text:
The models expand presets in an AfterValidator of the list's type (StreamNames, ProcessNames in config.py), so the strips, the layout switcher, the auto assigner and list-apps see plain names and need no changes. The Presets metadata of the type marks the option for the GUI's schema.

The entries as written stay on the model (_WithPresets.written(), a private attribute filled by a wrap validator), for what explains the configuration to people: check-config shows @browsers (firefox, librewolf, ...). The GUI edits the TOML document itself, not the models, so it always shows @browsers and writes it back as it was.

An apps strip with launch counts its applications as running when a process of theirs runs: before presets, the match entries were matched against the processes as they are. Now the plain entries still are, and each preset counts with its names for processes (AppsStripConfig.process_names), so @steam-games counts reaper, not .exe.

items.title: The presets
items.text:
Each is a short list of well-known applications, checked against what they report on a real system where possible (Brave, Mumble and a Proton game on this machine) and against their packages otherwise. Choices:

  • No broad names. steam (the client runs all the time), .exe in processes, chrome in processes (every Electron application runs a chrome_crashpad_handler), element (elementary OS's io.elementary.*), bare zen, jellyfin (the server is a process too), dragon (games). Tests list such names for each preset and fail if one matches them.
  • Streams can't tell who started a game. A Proton game from Steam and a Wine game from Lutris play alike, so the streams of @steam-games and @games are the same: every Windows program under Wine.
  • @games processes: reaper and wineserver. Lutris and Heroic leave no process of their own while a game runs (Lutris's lutris-wrapper names itself only with an optional Python module), so there is no reliable marker for them. wineserver runs while any Windows program runs under Wine or Proton, which on a desktop is mostly games, and a few seconds after it (which switching.hold covers anyway). Native games from Lutris or Heroic are not part of it.
  • Electron. Before Electron 40 every Electron application names its streams "Chromium" (with its own binary), so chromium in @browsers also takes their sounds, e.g. Discord's notifications. Leaving Chromium out of a browser preset would be worse; the docs say it.
  • REAPER. The digital audio workstation's process is reaper too, so @steam-games in processes also matches while it runs. Its users name their games in processes instead; the note of the preset says so.

The docs page lists every preset with its names; a test checks that its table is presets.markdown_table(), so it can't go stale.

items.title: Where presets show
items.text:
• check-config: each preset with what it stands for, in strips and layout rules.
  • list-apps: the presets each application that plays is part of (Brave (@browsers)), to find the right one.
  • The GUI: the options with the Presets metadata suggest the presets of their kind first (a "Presets" section of the menu, the description beside each, what it stands for as the tooltip), then the names of the sound server; a processes list, which had no suggestions, gets the presets for processes. The chip of a preset is outlined instead of filled and has the same tooltip.

items.title: Refactoring, November 2026
items.text:
A pass over the code for structure, without changing what anything does. The steps are ranked by value against risk; each is one commit, checked with ruff, pyright and the tests that cover it.

Status: all eight steps are done (2026-11-18).

items.title: Survey
items.text:
• 26 000 lines in src/. The layers hold: no Qt in gui/domain, nothing outside gui/ imports the GUI, pyright passes on src/.
  • The large modules: gui/qt/window/main_window.py (1100 lines), gui/qt/pages/slots.py (935), slots/model.py (785), gui/qt/preview/strip_view.py (700), runtime/daemon.py (640).
  • MainWindow builds the rail, the settings navigation, the menus, the header and the footer, filters the keys and the wheel of the whole application, decides which page shows a problem, and runs the service, the file, the zoom and "Try without a device".
  • SlotsPanel holds the widgets of a card (StackList, CandidateRow, the chips of a rule) next to the page, and decides in the widget what belongs to the domain: where a candidate stands against the one shown, which strip type the place of a candidate has, and what a pool hands out on a slot.
  • Dead code: demos.AUDIO_TYPES and Preview.drop_target are used nowhere.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Dead code. Remove demos.AUDIO_TYPES and Preview.drop_target.
  2. Decisions of the page Slots into the domain. slot_stacks gets row_state() (a candidate against the one shown), place_strip() (the strip type of a place) and member_summary() (what a pool hands out on a slot and who waits). The page calls them; they can be tested without Qt.
  3. The cards of the page Slots in a module of their own. gui/qt/pages/slot_cards.py gets StackList, CandidateRow, the chips and the rule of a candidate, and filling a card. pages/slots.py keeps the page: the bars, the inspector, Simulate and the edits.
  4. Where a problem is shown, in the domain. gui/domain/problems.py has place_of(problem): the page (and the channel, state or slot on it) that shows a problem. MainWindow.go_to() only goes there.
  5. The filter of the keys and the wheel. gui/qt/window/input_filter.py: the application-wide filter that keeps Undo and Redo from the text fields and the wheel from fields that would change their value. MainWindow installs it and removes it when it closes.
  6. The rail and the settings in a module of their own. gui/qt/window/rail.py: Rail (the pages, their names shown or not) and SettingsPages (the navigation and the stack of the settings). MainWindow keeps rail_buttons and nav_buttons for the tests and show_page().
  7. The geometry of a Session. The conversion between the pixels of the screen and those of the window is one function, scaled(), instead of written out twice.
  8. The files of the slots. runtime/slots.py keeps the SlotEngine; reading and writing slots.json and people.json go to runtime/slot_files.py.

After these, docs/development/architecture.md names the new modules.

items.title: Left as they are
items.text:
• runtime/daemon.py. One lifecycle: reload, preview and the run loop share the configuration that runs and the mixer. Splitting the preview off would hand the same state around, not make it simpler.
  • gui/qt/preview/strip_view.py. Long, but one thing: painting a strip and the hand on it. Its paint methods share the state of the strip and the cached pictures.
  • slots/model.py. The pydantic models of the configuration with their validators; the length is their docstrings, which the GUI shows as help.
  • strips/. The controller hierarchy is the extension point of the channel types; it is not duplicated.
  • The live protocol, the configuration format, the MQTT entities and the CLI. Untouched, as for any refactoring.
  • Tests that fail already. They are the owner's to fix; a test only gets a moved import.

items.title: Design: try changes and situations on the device
items.text: Status: built (2026-11-18).

items.title: Problem
items.text:
The GUI has two ways to see a configuration before it is real, and they don't know each other:

  • Try on the device (the live preview, live.StartPreview): the daemon runs the unsaved configuration of the editor instead of the file. The device follows every edit, but only in the situation there is right now.
  • Simulate on the page Slots: what the slots would show in another situation (another mode, states on or off, channels absent, so many people in the call, applications that play, devices without a channel). The resolver computes it in the GUI, only the drawing shows it, and nothing can be played: no daemon runs those strips.

Both answer "what would the device do if ...": with this configuration, and in this situation. Trying a situation on the device itself (the real one, or the virtual one) is what Simulate can't do.

items.title: Idea
items.text:
One preview with two optional parts, both run by the daemon:

  • the configuration: the editor's (unsaved changes), or the file;
  • the situation: the what-if of Simulate, or the real one.

The switch "Try on the device" (next to Save and apply) sends whatever differs from reality: the unsaved changes, and while Simulate is open, its situation too. With the switch off, Simulate stays what it is today: the drawing only. So the real device never changes without that switch (decision 1).

items.title: The situation in the daemon
items.text:
StartPreview gets an optional situation (slots.outcomes.Situation: mode, on, flipped, people, apps, devices, as gui.domain.simulate.WhatIf), and its config may be None: the file's configuration, in that situation.

The SlotEngine runs a situation in a second Simulation of its own (what_if), next to the real one:

  • States and the mode are overrides and the mode picked of that Simulation: each state of the scene is forced on or off as the situation says, the mode is picked. The real overrides and the mode picked are not touched.
  • Presence and the members come from an Observation made for the situation (Situation.observation): for a present apps channel an application its match takes, for an output/input channel its devices, for a person channel that person in the call; absent ones get none. The pools get their stand-ins: apps applications, people people, devices devices. Stand-ins are taken from what is real first (applications that play now, people in the call, devices without a channel), then made up (App 3, Person 2, Device 1): a real one has audio behind its strip, a made-up one shows its label on a strip that controls nothing.
  • Delays and dwells apply as in reality: a state switched on in the situation waits its on_delay, a channel that goes absent stays absent_after seconds. That is the point of trying it on the device.
  • The real Simulation is not stepped while a situation runs, and nothing of the situation is kept: no slots.json, no people.json.

engine.active is the Simulation that runs (the situation's, or the real one); the SlotMixer and the live view use it. Home Assistant keeps the real one: its slot sensors and state sensors are not updated while a situation runs, so automations never see a made-up situation. The live view tells simulated: true in the snapshot, with the slots and states of the situation.

What the device does on its own during a situation: the chord, Home Assistant's mode select and the overrides go to the real engine (they are real requests); the device shows the situation until it ends.

The situation ends with the preview: the switch off, Simulate ended (the configuration stays previewed if it has changes), the window closed or not answering for PREVIEW_TIMEOUT, the file changed. Then the real Simulation steps again at once and the slots show reality.

items.title: The GUI
items.text:
• Simulate with the switch on: the what-if goes to the daemon (debounced like edits), the drawing shows the live device (with the accent frame while the situation runs), the cards show the daemon's slots and their why, and Play works: the faders of real stand-ins move their audio.
  • Simulate with the switch off: as today, the resolver in the GUI, the drawing only, no Play. Its bar says "Only in the drawing: turn on Try on the device to run it on the device."
  • The switch is there while there are unsaved changes or Simulate is open, and a daemon can take it.
  • The pill next to it: "On the device, not saved", "On the device · simulated", "On the device, not saved · simulated", "Sending to the device…", "Paused: problems".
  • Esc ends Simulate as before; with the switch on the device goes back to the real situation.

items.title: Decisions (2026-11-18)
items.text:
1. Simulate drives the device only while "Try on the device" is on. Without it, nothing reaches the device.
  2. One preview in the daemon (configuration and situation), not a second mechanism: the same client, heartbeat, timeout, and ending.
  3. Stand-ins are real where they can be, made up otherwise.
  4. Home Assistant never sees a situation.

items.title: Not now
items.text:
• The chord and Home Assistant changing the situation instead of reality while one runs.
  • A banner on the device ("SIM") while a situation runs.

items.title: First steps
items.text: Set up the device, test it, write a configuration and run the daemon as a service. No device at hand? See Without a device.

items.title: Set up the device
items.text:
The extender has to be in MC (Mackie Control) mode on USB. Out of the box it may be set to the network interface: then it shows IP: 192.168.001.100 wait... and ignores USB.

  1. Switch it off.
  2. Hold the Select button of strip 1 and switch it on: the setup menu opens.
  3. Set Mode to MC and Interface to USB with the encoders.
  4. Leave the menu (Select of strip 1 again, or switch it off and on).

Connect it over USB. It needs no driver. Your user needs access to its MIDI device in /dev/snd: desktop sessions grant it to the logged-in user. Without a session, add the user to the audio group. See Hardware for details.

items.title: Test the device
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test

Every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader. Afterwards the command shows what you do on the device: faders, buttons and encoders. Ctrl+C stops it.

Only one program can use the device. Stop the daemon before the test (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon), and close DAWs that use it.

items.title: Write a configuration
items.text:
Without a configuration file the daemon uses the example configuration: six auto slots, the default input and the default output. To change it, write the example to ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml and edit it:

xtouch-daemon init-config     # writes ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml
xtouch-daemon list-devices    # the names to use for device channels, and the profiles of the sound cards
xtouch-daemon list-apps       # the applications that play now, and which channel or slot takes them
xtouch-daemon check-config    # validates the file and shows what each slot shows when

A channel is something a strip can control, a slot is a strip of the device, and states (in a call, gaming) decide what each slot shows. For example:

[channel.buds]
type = "output"
device = "bluez_output.4C_D7_3A_EA_02_76.1"
label = "Buds"
color = "green"

[channel.voip]
type = "apps"
match = ["@voip"]   # Discord, Mumble, TeamSpeak and more, see Presets
label = "VoIP"

[state.call]
voice_chat = true   # in a channel of Mumble (with the plugin)

[slots]
1 = ["buds if present", "auto"]
2 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
# slots 3 to 8 have no entry: "auto", the next application that plays

Channels, states and slots explains the format, Configuration every option. The GUI (xtouch-daemon gui) edits it in a window; see GUI.

items.title: Run it as a service
items.text:
xtouch-daemon install-service --now

This writes the systemd user unit ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service, enables it and starts it. From now on it starts with your session. Without --now it only writes the unit.

The Arch Linux package has its own unit, so with it the command writes nothing: it enables and starts the unit of the package. The same without the command:

systemctl --user enable --now xtouch-daemon

A unit in ~/.config/systemd/user (e.g. from an installation from the source) overrides the one of the package. xtouch-daemon install-service --remove-override removes it, so does "Use the packaged unit" in the GUI.

Task Command Apply a changed configuration xtouch-daemon check-config && systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon Restart (after changing [mqtt]) systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon Stop (e.g. for xtouch-daemon test) systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon See whether the device, sound server and broker are connected systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon Follow the log journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f

To run it in the foreground instead, e.g. to watch the log while you try something:

xtouch-daemon run -l debug

items.title: Arch Linux
items.text:
The AUR has two packages, built from the releases:

Package Contents xtouch-daemon-bin The daemon with its own Python 3.14 in /usr/lib/xtouch-daemon, the command xtouch-daemon, the systemd user unit /usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service and the example configuration /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/config.example.toml. xtouch-daemon-gui-bin The GUI, xtouch-daemon-gui, with a menu entry. It runs on the system's Python and PyQt6, and needs xtouch-daemon-bin of the same version.

Install them with an AUR helper, e.g.:

paru -S xtouch-daemon-bin xtouch-daemon-gui-bin

Then enable the service, see Run it as a service. After an upgrade, restart it (systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon): it runs the old version until then.

items.title: From the source
items.text:
xtouch-daemon uses haad-mqtt-autodiscovery from a checkout next to its own. Clone both side by side and install with uv:

git clone https://github.com/markusressel/xtouch-daemon
git clone https://github.com/haad-org/haad-mqtt-autodiscovery
uv tool install ./xtouch-daemon

uv installs Python 3.14 if your system does not have it. The command xtouch-daemon is then on your PATH.

For the GUI, install the gui extra instead. It brings Qt along, so it needs no system packages:

uv tool install --force './xtouch-daemon[gui]'

items.title: The GUI
items.text:
The GUI comes with xtouch-daemon-gui-bin (Arch Linux) or the gui extra (from the source), see above. It starts with xtouch-daemon-gui (the package, also "X-Touch Extender" in the menu of the desktop) or xtouch-daemon gui (from the source):

xtouch-daemon-gui            # the default configuration file
xtouch-daemon-gui -c FILE    # another one

Without the extra, xtouch-daemon gui says how to install it.

Next: First steps.

items.title: Without a device
items.text:
A virtual X-Touch Extender stands in for the device, e.g. to try a configuration or while the device is away:

xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device   # or [device] virtual = true
xtouch-daemon gui

While the daemon waits for it, the pill on the bar of the window Device in the GUI says "virtual device not running · Open it": a click opens it, and the mouse on the drawing is a hand on the device (see GUI). Without a daemon running, "Try without a device" above the drawing does both at once (see GUI). xtouch-daemon virtual-device runs one without the GUI. The virtual device speaks the bytes of the real one, so the daemon does the same with it, down to faders that wait for a touch; Hardware lists what it does like the device and what is assumed.

A daemon that runs but finds no device switches to the virtual one without a restart: "Use the virtual device" above the drawing sets [device] virtual = true, saves and opens it, and Play on a daemon that waits for the virtual device opens it too. Setting virtual back to false and saving switches to the real device again.

items.title: GUI
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui edits the configuration file in a window and applies it to the running daemon. It starts with xtouch-daemon-gui (the Arch Linux package) or xtouch-daemon gui, -c FILE for another file; see Install.

It edits channels, states and slots.

items.title: The window
items.text:
The window Configuration has a rail of four pages on its left, icons only (» at its foot shows their names, « hides them again; the GUI remembers it):

  • Slots: what each slot shows when, see The slots.
  • Channels: the channels of the file, then the built-in pools [pool.apps], [pool.people], [pool.auto] and [pool.devices]. Add (by type), Duplicate and Remove; the id can be renamed. Each says where it is used (slot 2, pool games, state call).
  • States: the modes first, then the other states. The form asks in order: State or Mode (a mode has a label and a priority), and On while: Sources or Condition, never both. Sources lists only the ones the state has, each with ✕ to remove it; Add source offers the others ("An application plays", "You are in the voice chat", ...), and the state is on while any of them is. Condition takes a condition of other states and modes, in the field of the page Slots. Switching between them asks before it removes what the other had. Delays and overrides (delay_on, delay_off, persist) are folded away until a state has one. Above the form: what the daemon says about it right now (since when, from which source), its override (a mode: picked by hand), and which stacks and controls use it.
  • Settings: [behavior], [aliases], [mqtt] (as "Home Assistant"), [switching] (as "Modes and chord"), [voip] (as "Voice chat") and [device]. "Voice chat" also tells whether Mumble is connected, lists the steps of its setup, and installs the Mumble plugin with "Install Mumble plugin".

Slots, Channels and States have a list or the slots on the left and what is picked on the right. The handle between them (the short upright bar) gives either side more room; each page keeps its share for the next start.

The window Device shows the device on every page, above the window Configuration at first. The title bar of either moves it to another side of the window, next to the other one, or out of it as a window of its own (e.g. on another screen); View → Device closes and opens the device (Configuration always stays open). The GUI keeps where they are for the next start. Clicking a strip of it (or Left, Right, Home, End) shows its slot on the page Slots.

The drawing of the device shows the encoder with its ring of 13 LEDs (Mackie Control lights the middle 11), the LCD (the backlight in the strip's color shines around a dark panel and through its characters, as on the device), the meter next to Rec, Solo, Mute and Select, and the fader with its dB scale: the middle of the cap marks the value, -∞ at the bottom, 0 dB at 77 % of the travel (behavior.unity_at). What each slot shows is printed under its LCD.

The footer shows the problems, whether the device runs the file, the switch Try on the device while there are unsaved changes, and the buttons Undo, Redo, Revert and "Save and apply". The title of the window names the file, with • while there are unsaved changes. The header has the state of the service with buttons to install, start, restart or stop it (see The service), and what the sound server has.

Help where you look: while the mouse is on something with a tooltip, the footer shows its first sentence at once, in place of the status line; the tooltip itself follows after a moment, with the states, channels and slots it names in their colors. A pill with ▾ opens what it means in full on a click, with what can be done about it: a row per thing, with a bar in the color of how it does (a problem is also tinted and its fix is the main button). A control that is off says why next to it (e.g. "Play: device not connected").

States, channels and slots have a color each, in the whole window: states (and modes) violet, channels (and what else a slot can show: pools, people) teal, slots orange. The icons of their pages on the rail, the chips of the slots, the state bar and the words and sections in the help ([state.gaming], "the slot", "an application", apps) have them; a condition of presence (present) is yellow. The controls of the device (Select, Mute, the fader, the encoder, ...) stand out from the help in the color of the text.

Lists and pages that scroll cast a soft shadow at an edge where more of them is hidden, and popovers a shadow on the window under them.

The menus have what is used now and then: File (Save and apply, Revert, Quit), Edit (Undo, Redo), View (the window Device, the dark or the light theme, the zoom) and Help (this documentation).

items.title: The service
items.text:
The service button installs, starts and restarts the systemd user service, the same as xtouch-daemon install-service. It asks before it installs or starts it. While the service runs, "Stop" next to it stops it (systemctl --user stop): it stays enabled, so it starts again with the next session, or with "Start".

A daemon that runs outside systemd (e.g. from a terminal or an IDE) is found too: the header shows "running elsewhere", and saving reloads it. The GUI does not start, restart or stop that one: restart it where it runs.

Next to the state of the service, the header shows which unit systemd uses: "packaged" for the one of the Arch Linux package (/usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service), or "own unit" for a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user, which install-service wrote, e.g. for a checkout; its tooltip has the unit and the program it starts.

  • Install and start takes the unit of the package when the GUI is the one of the package: it enables and starts it, and writes no file. Any other GUI writes a unit for its own xtouch-daemon to ~/.config/systemd/user.
  • Use the packaged unit shows while a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user overrides the one of the package. It removes that file; an enabled service stays enabled, and a running one restarts with the program of the package.
  • Restart stands out (with a tooltip that names both versions) when the daemon runs another version than the one installed, e.g. after an upgrade of the package: the daemon keeps running the old version until it restarts. This needs a daemon that tells its version (0.1.0 and later), and only counts for the service of the installation the GUI runs from.

items.title: Zoom
items.text:
Ctrl++ (or Ctrl+=) makes the whole window larger, Ctrl+- smaller, Ctrl+0 goes back to 100 %; View → Zoom has the levels from 67 % to 300 %. The GUI keeps the zoom for the next start, like the theme.

Qt scales a window only when it opens, so a new zoom opens the window again at the new size: unsaved changes, undo, the selected slot and the page stay. The zoom is on top of a QT_SCALE_FACTOR of the environment.

items.title: Live view
items.text:
While the daemon runs, the drawing shows what the device shows right now ("Live", in a pill on the right of the bar of the window Device), read from the daemon's live view. Without a running daemon it is dark, and the window says so. A daemon that runs while the device is not connected shows "Live · not connected": the strips show what the device will show once it is there.

With the virtual device (run --virtual-device), the pill says "Live · virtual device" once the daemon drives it, and "virtual device not running · Open it" while the daemon waits for it: a click opens it in the window (see below).

Next to it, a pill shows the mode the device shows ("Mode: gaming", "No mode" while no mode is on, "· by hand" when it was picked by hand). A mode is a state with mode = true: one at a time is on. A click lists the states, with what turned each on, and picks a mode by hand ("Pick gaming", "Pick no mode", "Back to the rules").

The pill of the service at the top tells what the daemon is connected to: "running" while all is well, else the worst problem, e.g. "running · Home Assistant not authorized" or "running · device not connected". A click lists each connection (the device, the sound server, Home Assistant with an [mqtt] section, the voice chat with [voip]), how it is doing and why (for Home Assistant the broker's own words and what to check), with a button to its settings.

items.title: Select and Play
items.text:
A bar above the drawing of the device switches what the mouse does on it:

  • Select: a click picks a strip, and with it its slot on the page Slots. Dragging a strip moves its slot to another place: the strip lifts out of the row, the others glide aside, and a dashed place shows where it goes; Escape puts it back. Ctrl+Left/Right and the context menu (Move left, Move right) do the same. A slot takes its candidates ([slots]) and its controls ([controls]) along, the slots in between make room; Ctrl+Z moves it back. Comments above the slots in the file stay where they are.
  • Play: the mouse is a hand on the device:
  • a fader: press to touch it, drag to move it, release to let go; Alt-drag moves it without a touch, like the device moving it by itself (the daemon puts it back);
  • a button: held while the mouse button is down;
  • an encoder: the wheel turns it, a click pushes it.

Play works on the virtual device the window hosts, and on the device of a running daemon: then the daemon takes what the mouse does as if the device sent it, so the mixer acts and a motorized fader follows once it is let go. The fader under the mouse is drawn there at once. Play is off while Simulate shows only the drawing (it works when Simulate runs on the device, see Try on the device), without a daemon (or with one of another user, or too old to take it) and while the device is not connected; the bar says why next to it ("Play: device not connected"). With a daemon that drives the virtual device ([device] virtual = true) while it doesn't run, Play opens it in the window and plays on it.

While no daemon runs, "Try without a device" starts one with the virtual device on this file (saved first if it is new) and opens the device in the window, in Play: to set everything up and try it before there is a device. That daemon ends with the window.

items.title: The virtual device
items.text:
While the window hosts the virtual device, Play is on (see Select and Play).

A bar above the drawing unplugs it and plugs it in again, switches it off and on (the faders go down by themselves, as on the device), and breaks the touch sensor of faders ("Broken touch"), to try touchless_faders. "Close" closes it, and so does closing the window: for the daemon it is unplugged. What the drawing shows still comes from the daemon, which is what reached the device.

items.title: Try on the device
items.text:
Next to Save and apply, a pill says what the device runs: "Saved, on the device", "Unsaved changes" (the device runs the saved file), "On the device, not saved", or what is wrong (e.g. "Not running", "Not on the device yet"). A click tells it in full, with the path of the file ("Copy the path", "Open the folder") and the file the daemon reads when that is another one.

While there are unsaved changes, the switch "Try on the device" sits next to it: the device runs the configuration in the editor before it is saved, and follows every change a moment after it (undo and redo too). The file is not written. Without unsaved changes the switch is gone: the device runs the file anyway. Once on, it stays on for the next changes until it is turned off or the window closes; a new window starts with it off.

  • While it is on, the pill says "On the device, not saved" ("Sending to the device…" for a moment after a change).
  • Save and apply makes it the configuration: the daemon loads the saved file, which is what the device shows already.
  • Back to the file: turning the switch off, closing the window (it asks about unsaved changes as usual, and says that the device runs them) or "Revert" brings back the saved file. So does a window that crashed: the daemon goes back to the file when the connection of the window ends, or when the window does not answer for 10 seconds. The file also comes back when it changes on disk, or the daemon is reloaded; then the switch goes off and the window says why.
  • What the daemon does not take shows in red under the status bar at the top, and the device keeps the version before. It can't change [mqtt] (that takes a save and a restart), nor [device] name and virtual (they take a save). A configuration with problems is not sent at all: the pill says "Paused: problems" until they are fixed.
  • Channels, states and slots are all part of it: a stack changed in the editor shows on the device as it is.
  • Simulate on the device: while Simulate is open on the page Slots, the switch is there too (also without unsaved changes), and turned on, the device shows the what-if of Simulate instead of what really happens, with the changes if there are any: the states and the mode it sets, its channels present or absent, and its people, applications and devices (real ones first, so their faders move real audio; made-up ones for the rest, App 1, Device 1). Delays and dwells apply as they really do. The drawing shows the device then, the cards the daemon's slots and why, Play works, and the pill says "On the device · simulated". Ending Simulate (Esc) shows what really happens again. Home Assistant never sees it: its slot and state sensors stay as they really are, and nothing of it is kept. With the switch off, Simulate only draws; its bar says "Only in the drawing".
  • One window at a time: a second window that turns it on takes over, and the first one's switch goes off.
  • Home Assistant: channels the changes do not have keep their entities in Home Assistant (with their state; only nothing drives them), so they are as before once the file runs again. Entities of channels only the changes had are removed again when it ends.

The switch is disabled, and its label says why ("Try on the device: no daemon"), while no daemon runs, while the daemon reads another file, and for a daemon from before this feature (restart it to run the installed version).

items.title: The slots
items.text:
On the page Slots:

  • The state bar lists the states and modes: ● on, ○ off, with the override in brackets. A click on one shows what turned it on, its override (real, like Home Assistant or xtouch-daemon mode: auto, on, off, or for a mode picking it and back to the rules), and Simulate with it the other way (nothing changes).
  • A card per slot lists its candidates as rules, read from the top like "if, else if, else": the first whose condition holds wins. when gaming → auto shows auto while gaming is on, otherwise → browser below it browser the rest of the time (always for a lone candidate without a condition). A pool without a condition reads when app without a slot → apps (an outlined chip): it shows only while it has a member no other slot has, else the slot goes on to the next candidate. A tiny LCD after what it shows has the color of the strip: the candidate's own color, else the channel's or the pool's, else white (two for auto: applications and people; one per color for a pool of channels; dark for -). Its tooltip says where the color comes from. A rail on the left joins the candidates from the top, with "else" between two and a node on each: green on the one the device shows (or Simulate would). Above it, the candidates are dimmed with why they did not win (✗ browser doesn't play, ✗ browser is on slot 3); below it, dimmed more: not reached. When none of them has anything to show (e.g. the last is a pool with no member left), all are dimmed with why (✗ no person without a slot) and the rail ends in a row of its own, "nothing to show: the strip is dark", which is the one shown. On the one shown, the chip of a pool names what it hands out there (apps · firefox, people · Alice), and its tooltip who else waits for a slot. A card that gets a line more or less grows or shrinks smoothly. Conditions are outlined chips, what the slot shows a filled one. The states are violet (call, not gaming, one per or). present is spelled out in an olive chip (green in the light theme), in what it means for the type of the channel or pool: browser if present reads when browser plays → browser, mic if present mic is connected, mum if present mum is in the voice chat, present(people) someone is in the voice chat. What the slot shows is teal (see the colors), and the green node is on the row that shows (on people while a person sits there, also when apps is above it). Options of the strip in that slot only follow as in the file (color = white, rec = recording). + adds auto at the end, the bin removes the candidate picked. Drag a candidate, or move it with Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down. A slot without candidates shows auto.
  • The inspector starts with the path of the slot's candidates (Slot 3 › 1 games › 2 apps: the one picked highlighted, ● the one the slot shows, ○ the one it came to that has none left; a click picks one) and a box of what goes on: why the slot shows what it shows, a step a line (✗ a candidate passed over and why, → what it shows, the same as xtouch-daemon why 3), which channel the candidate shows, where else that is used and where it is now, or what a pool hands out and from which side, with "Edit the channel" to its page, and what [controls] claims of the slot. Below it, it edits the candidate picked: what it shows (a channel, a pool such as apps, people or auto, -), when (the condition: states violet, channels in present(...) teal, a mistake underlined in red with what is wrong in its tooltip; typing offers the states, keywords and channels that fit, Ctrl+Space all of them), and the options of its place (look, on apps and auto the encoder and the volume range, on people the look of a person's strip).

Clicking a strip in the window Device (or Left, Right, Home, End) picks its card, with the candidate it shows.

Simulate shows what the slots would show in another mode, with other states on, with channels absent (auto plays: an application plays; people fill, apps fill: as many as there are slots), or with so many people in the call and applications that play (the two counts; the strips show their names): a frame goes around the drawing in the window Device, a bar of what-ifs replaces the state bar, and the drawing, the cards and the box of the inspector follow it. With "Try on the device" on, the device shows it too (see Try on the device); else nothing is sent to the daemon. Esc, or Simulate again, ends it.

items.title: Editing options
items.text:
The forms come from the options of the configuration, so every option has a field. The options of a channel are in cards in the order of the device, from top to bottom: what it controls, the encoder, the display, the buttons (Rec, Solo, Mute, Select), the fader and the meter, then those about slots (tags, in_pool, ...).

The cards of the encoder, the display, the buttons and the fader have a drawing of that part of the strip, which shows what the options do on the device in a few steps (‹ and › go through them), each with a caption: the ring as the encoder turns and is pushed, the LCD while audio plays, while muted and with nothing to control, which LEDs light while audio plays, an application records or the strip is muted, and the volume at the bottom, at the 0 dB mark and at the top of the fader, with what the meter shows there. It follows the values in the form at once, saved or not, at the step shown.

  • switches for on/off options, numbers with their ranges, choices, color swatches, lists as chips, masked fields for secrets, and file pickers;
  • the help of each option under its field, with its default and, where the documentation explains more, a "Learn more" link to that section; a button sets the option back to its default;
  • choices as a table, with the devices, the sound cards and the profiles of the card of each line to pick from. While a channel has choices, device and profiles are hidden, and the other way around: a channel has one or the other;
  • for choices, what the chosen value does (e.g. recording for the Rec LED), and each value says it as a tooltip in the list;
  • the mouse wheel scrolls the page, also over a number or a choice: it never changes a value;
  • the errors next to the options they belong to, with the same messages as xtouch-daemon check-config. The problems button in the footer lists them all; a click opens the page of the problem. An unknown option can be removed from there.

[mqtt] can be added and removed on its page. Above its options, the page shows how the daemon's connection is doing (or that the daemon runs without the section, which it reads only when it starts), and "Test connection" connects once with the settings as they are in the editor, saved or not, and says what is wrong if that fails.

items.title: Suggestions from the sound server
items.text:
The GUI reads the sound server and suggests what it has:

Option Suggestions device The outputs or inputs by node name, with their descriptions; the default is marked. profiles The profiles of the sound cards of those devices; the active one is marked. match, exclude of [pool.apps], apps and recording of a state The presets (@browsers, ...) first, then the names and binaries of the applications that play. A preset's tooltip tells what it stands for; its chip is outlined. processes of a state The presets for processes. [aliases] The names of the applications that play. person of a person channel The people in the voice chat now, as the running daemon tells them.

The pill "Sound server: ..." says how much the GUI read; a click lists the outputs, inputs and applications, with "Read again" (also the refresh button next to it), e.g. after you started an application. Without a sound server, type the names by hand. The people of the voice chat come from the daemon's live view: without a running daemon (or nobody in the channel), type the names by hand.

items.title: Undo
items.text:
Every edit can be undone: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes. That includes removing a channel and reverting the file, so neither asks first. Typing into one option is one step. Ctrl+Z undoes in the document also while a text field has the focus.

Closing the window with unsaved changes asks whether to save them.

items.title: Save and apply
items.text:
"Save and apply" (Ctrl+S) writes the file and reloads the daemon:

  • It saves only a file without problems: the daemon would not take one with problems.
  • Unchanged values keep their place and their comments, and a stack keeps its form (a string, a list, tables) where it did not change. The file is written in place, so a symlinked configuration stays one.
  • It reloads the running daemon when that reads the saved file: the service, or one started from a terminal or an IDE.
  • Without changes it is there too while the daemon runs another version of the file, e.g. one edited outside the GUI: then it only reloads the daemon.
  • A changed [mqtt] section is not reloaded at all: the window offers "Restart the service" for the service; restart a daemon that runs elsewhere where it runs. A changed [device] name or virtual is: the daemon switches to that device.
  • It then tells whether the device runs the saved file: "The device runs the saved file", or "The device does not run the saved file yet". If that stays, the daemon did not take the file, and its log says why (journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon).

"Revert" drops the changes and reads the file again (Undo brings them back).

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text: A homeassistant strip belongs to Home Assistant instead of PipeWire: every part of it is an entity there, and automations decide what it does. For example, the fader dims a light, the encoder sets the volume of a speaker in another room, a button toggles a scene. The daemon reaches Home Assistant over MQTT discovery, so it needs the [mqtt] section.

items.title: PipeWire or Home Assistant?
items.text: Each control has one owner. The PipeWire types (output, input, apps, auto) control audio on this computer and need nothing else. A homeassistant strip controls nothing by itself; it only reports what happens on it and shows what Home Assistant sets. In between, an audio strip can hand its fader or its encoder to Home Assistant and keep the other one for the volume, see below. Never both on one control: a fader that both set a PipeWire volume and were moved by Home Assistant would fight over the motor.

items.title: [mqtt]
items.text:
The MQTT broker of Home Assistant, e.g. the Mosquitto add-on. Without homeassistant strips the section is optional; with it, the daemon connects anyway and shows the device in Home Assistant.

Option Default Meaning host required The broker, e.g. "homeassistant.local". port 1883 Its port. username none The user to log in as. password none The password, in the file. password_file none A file that holds the password instead, e.g. one only you can read. ~ is the home directory. Surrounding whitespace is ignored. password_env none An environment variable that holds the password instead, e.g. set with systemctl --user edit xtouch-daemon (Environment=). discovery_prefix "homeassistant" Home Assistant's MQTT discovery prefix. namespace "xtouch" Starts every entity ID (number.xtouch_lamp_fader) and is part of the topics. Lower case letters, digits, _. device_name "X-Touch Extender" The name of the device in Home Assistant.

Set at most one of password, password_file and password_env. A password file that can't be read, or a variable that is not set, stops the daemon at the start with a message.

[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_file = "~/.config/xtouch-daemon/mqtt-password"

A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart of the daemon (systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon). Until then, a reload keeps the whole current configuration.

The entities are available in Home Assistant while the daemon runs and the device is connected; otherwise they are greyed out. A last will covers a crash. The daemon connects to the broker again by itself when it was gone.

The GUI shows whether the daemon is connected, and why not (e.g. a wrong password), and its "Test connection" button tries settings before they are saved.

items.title: homeassistant channels
items.text:
Option Default Meaning type required "homeassistant". label none The top line of the LCD until Home Assistant sets one, and the start of the entity names (the id without it). color "white" The LCD color until Home Assistant sets one. 
[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_env = "XTOUCH_MQTT_PASSWORD"

[channel.living_room]
type = "homeassistant"   # number.xtouch_living_room_fader, ...
label = "Living"
color = "yellow"

[slots]
8 = "living_room"

The entities belong to the channel, not to a slot: they stay in Home Assistant whichever slot shows the channel, and while none does.

items.title: Audio strips with Home Assistant controls
items.text:
An output, input or apps channel, or an auto place, with encoder = "homeassistant" or fader = "homeassistant" keeps the volume on the other control and gets these entities of the list below:

Option Entities encoder = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_encoder, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with encoder_pressed, encoder_released. fader = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_fader, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with fader_touched, fader_released.

The LCD, the LEDs and the buttons stay with PipeWire. The channel's id names the entities, its label starts their names. See Encoders for the details.

[channel.desk]
type = "output"
device = "alsa_output.usb-*"
label = "Desk"
encoder = "homeassistant"    # the fader sets the volume, the encoder dims the desk lamp

A control of a slot can belong to Home Assistant whatever the slot shows, with [controls]: 6 = { fader = "homeassistant", id = "desk" } is number.xtouch_desk_fader.

items.title: Entities
items.text:
<ns> is mqtt.namespace, <id> the id of the channel (desk for [channel.desk]) or the id of the control:

Entity What it is number.<ns>_<id>_fader The fader, 0..100 in steps of 0.1. Setting it moves the motor fader; moving the fader by hand sets it (at most every 100 ms while it moves, and where it was let go). number.<ns>_<id>_encoder The encoder, 0..100. The ring shows it; turning the encoder changes it by behavior.encoder_step per step. number.<ns>_<id>_meter The LED meter, 0..100 %: 0 is dark, 100 lights it fully; the daemon holds the level (the device would let it fall). Its 14 levels are about 7 % each, 100 % lights the red LED at the top too, so e.g. a CPU load or a power ratio goes in as it is. text.<ns>_<id>_top, text.<ns>_<id>_bottom The two lines of the LCD, 7 characters each. select.<ns>_<id>_color The LCD color: off, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white. select.<ns>_<id>_rec_led, _solo_led, _mute_led, _select_led The LEDs of the buttons: off, on or flash. event.<ns>_<id>_buttons What happens on the strip: rec_pressed, rec_released, solo_…, mute_…, select_…, encoder_pressed, encoder_released, fader_touched, fader_released.

A button does not switch its LED: if a button should toggle something, an automation reacts to the event and sets the LED to show the result. Home Assistant keeps what it set last (retained on the broker), so after a restart of the daemon the strips show it again. New entities start with the configured label and color, the fader and encoder at 0 and the LEDs off. While the broker can't be reached, a strip shows its label, offline and its color, and the device does nothing on it.

Entities of a channel that was removed from the configuration are removed from Home Assistant on the next reload.

items.title: Choices
items.text:
With [mqtt], an output or input channel with choices has select.<ns>_<id>_output (select.<ns>_<id>_input): the choice the strip shows, one option per choice, named by its label (or its device; a second choice of the same name gets a number, e.g. Out 2). Choosing one switches to it like Select on the device, profile first; one that isn't there is refused and the select goes back. The select follows the strip, also when the default changes elsewhere.

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_out_output
data:
  option: Speaker

items.title: Modes, states and slots
items.text:
With [mqtt], Home Assistant sees and sets the states and modes:

Entity What it is select.<ns>_mode The mode picked by hand, or auto for the rules. Choosing one picks it, like xtouch-daemon mode. binary_sensor.<ns>_state_<id> Each state and mode, with the attributes since, source and override. select.<ns>_state_<id> The override of each state that is no mode: auto, on, off. switch.<ns>_state_<id>_input For states with homeassistant = true: what Home Assistant feeds into them. binary_sensor.<ns>_<id>_shown Whether a channel is on a slot. sensor.<ns>_slot_<n> What slot n shows (a channel id, app:<name>, person:<name> or none), with label, kind, via and reason.

For example, the mode gaming while the PC runs a game, from another room's automation:

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_mode
data:
  option: gaming

items.title: Automations
items.text:
An automation that dims a light with the fader, shows its brightness on the LCD, and toggles it with Mute:

automation:
  - alias: "X-Touch: fader dims the living room"
    mode: queued
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_fader
    actions:
      - action: light.turn_on
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }
        data:
          brightness_pct: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}"
      - action: text.set_value
        target: { entity_id: text.xtouch_living_room_bottom }
        data:
          value: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}%"

  - alias: "X-Touch: Mute toggles the living room"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: event.xtouch_living_room_buttons
        attribute: event_type
        to: mute_pressed
    actions:
      - action: light.toggle
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }

  - alias: "X-Touch: the Mute LED shows the living room light"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: light.living_room
    actions:
      - action: select.select_option
        target: { entity_id: select.xtouch_living_room_mute_led }
        data:
          option: "{{ 'on' if is_state('light.living_room', 'on') else 'off' }}"

  - alias: "X-Touch: the meter shows the power of the washing machine"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.washing_machine_power
    actions:
      - action: number.set_value
        target: { entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_meter }
        data:
          # 2000 W lights it fully
          value: "{{ [trigger.to_state.state | float(0) / 2000 * 100, 100] | min | round(0) }}"

items.title: haad
items.text:
The same as a haad controller (a sketch: the entity wrappers are haad's, the names depend on your setup):

@haad_controller(registry_name="xtouch_living_room")
class XTouchLivingRoom(HaadController):
    @haad_ha_entity
    def fader(self) -> HANumber:
        return HANumber("number.xtouch_living_room_fader")

    @haad_ha_entity
    def encoder(self) -> HANumber:
        return HANumber("number.xtouch_living_room_encoder")

    @haad_ha_entity
    def buttons(self) -> HAEventEntity:
        return HAEventEntity("event.xtouch_living_room_buttons")

    @haad_ha_entity
    def light(self) -> HALight:
        return HALight("light.living_room")

    @haad_ha_entity
    def speaker(self) -> HAMediaPlayer:
        return HAMediaPlayer("media_player.living_room")

    async def initialize(self) -> None:
        async def dim() -> None:
            # turn_on() of HALight does nothing for a light that is on: set the brightness directly
            brightness = await self.fader.get_state()
            await self.ha.perform_action("light/turn_on", entity_id=self.light.entity_id, brightness_pct=brightness)

        async def volume() -> None:
            await self.speaker.volume_set(await self.encoder.get_state() / 100)

        async def button() -> None:
            if await self.buttons.get_event_type() == "mute_pressed":
                await self.light.toggle()

        await self.react_to(trigger=self.fader, action=dim)
        await self.react_to(trigger=self.encoder, action=volume)
        await self.react_to(trigger=self.buttons, action=button)

items.title: Mumble
items.text:
With the Mumble plugin of xtouch-daemon, the strips of people show the people in your Mumble channel, one per strip:

  • the name on the LCD, the backlight in talking_color while they talk, and their voice on the meter;
  • the fader sets their volume for you (0 to 200 %, max_volume at the top);
  • Mute mutes them for you: it is Mumble's own local mute, so Mumble shows it, and a local mute you set in Mumble lights the button;
  • people who join or leave the channel, and you moving to another channel, show at once.

It needs Mumble 1.4 or later on Linux (x86_64). People sit on the slots of auto (and people) in every configuration; the [voip] section can be left out: its provider = "bridge" is the default.

items.title: Setup in the GUI
items.text:
The page "Voice chat" of the global settings (the [voip] section) has a box "Mumble":

  1. Click Install Mumble plugin. It copies the plugin into Mumble's plugin directory (~/.local/share/Mumble/Mumble/Plugins, or the one of the Flatpak), replacing an older one. (Without a plugin to install, e.g. in a checkout, the button builds it first; that needs cmake and a C compiler.) Mumble's own installer is not used: with a Mumble that runs, it starts a second instance, which crashed (Mumble 1.5.939).
  2. In Mumble: Settings, Plugins, click Reload plugins (or restart Mumble), tick Enable of "xtouch-daemon", and Apply.
  3. Keep provider = "bridge" (the default). People take free auto slots from the right; see the example below.
  4. Join a channel. The pill of the box says Mumble connected and how many people are in the channel.

The pill shows what the running daemon sees: "waiting for Mumble" while the plugin is not connected (Mumble is not running, or the plugin is not enabled), "not in use" for a daemon older than the people of auto.

items.title: Setup on the command line
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --install

does what the button does (see mumble-plugin); then step 2 above. Without xtouch-daemon's help: in Mumble, Settings, Plugins, Install plugin..., and pick /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a release) or integrations/mumble/build/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a checkout, after xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build).

items.title: Slots for Mumble
items.text:
Alice always on slot 1 while she is there, the others on the auto slots from the right, and Mumble as one strip with your microphone while you are in a channel:

[channel.alice]
type = "person"
person = "Alice"      # her name in Mumble

[channel.voip]
type = "apps"
match = ["mumble"]
label = "Mumble"

[channel.mic]
type = "input"

[state.call]
voice_chat = true     # in a channel of Mumble
delay_off = 5

[slots]
1 = ["alice if present", "auto"]
6 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
7 = ["mic if call", "auto"]

See People and the voice chat and States and modes.

To start Mumble from the device, give a slot a launch in [controls] with a mumble:// URL, e.g. 6 = { select = { launch = ["mumble", "mumble://me@voice.example.org/Gaming"] }, when = "not call" }: Select starts Mumble, which connects to the server and joins the channel. See Launching the application.

items.title: What it does, and what not
items.text:
• Mute is Mumble's "Local Mute" (in the menu of a user): Mute on the strip sets it, Mumble shows it in its window, and setting it in Mumble lights the button. Mumble tells plugins of no change of the local mute, so the plugin looks every half second: a mute set in Mumble reaches the button within about 0.5 s (a press of Mute on the strip shows at once). Should Mumble refuse a mute, the button goes back, and Mumble's log says why ("xtouch-daemon: can't mute ..."). A local mute set from the strip lasts while the person stays; Mumble only stores the ones set in its own menu (for registered users).
  • The volume is the plugin's own. The plugin scales the voice of each person before Mumble mixes it. Mumble's own "Local Volume Adjustment" is separate, and the faders don't show or change it: Mumble's plugin interface has no call for it. The two multiply: a person at 50 % in Mumble and 50 % on the fader is at 25 %.
  • The daemon keeps them for the name. The plugin forgets the volume of someone who leaves; the daemon remembers the volume and the mute the strips set for each name while it runs and sends them again when the person comes back (a mute changed in Mumble meanwhile replaces the one of the strip). A restart of the daemon starts everyone at 100 %.
  • Not their own mute. Whether other people muted or deafened themselves is not in Mumble's plugin interface: it tells their talking state only, and someone who muted themselves sends nothing, so they just don't talk.
  • Your channel only, without you: nobody else's channel, no whispers to other channels.
  • The level on the meter is the voice as it arrives, before or after the fader (meter_point), and before Mumble's own volume and positional audio. Mumble does not fetch the voice of a muted person: before the fader their meter lights while they talk, without a level; after it, it stays dark.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The plugin (integrations/mumble/plugin.c, plugin API 1.0) connects to the socket of the daemon, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock, and speaks the bridge protocol: the people of the channel on every change and 20 times a second while someone talks (for the levels), and the volume and mute commands back. The plugin's socket thread never calls into Mumble; a second thread makes the calls for the mute, which Mumble runs in its main thread (see the comment at the top of plugin.c). It connects again every 2 seconds while the daemon is not there, so the order in which Mumble and the daemon start does not matter. $XTOUCH_DAEMON_VOIP_SOCKET (in Mumble's environment) points it to another socket.

Flatpak: a Mumble in a Flatpak can't see the socket by default. Let it:

flatpak override --user --filesystem=xdg-run/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock info.mumble.Mumble

items.title: Building it
items.text:
cmake -S integrations/mumble -B integrations/mumble/build
cmake --build integrations/mumble/build

makes libxtouch-daemon.so and the bundle xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (the library and a manifest.xml, as Mumble installs plugins), the same as xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build. The releases have it built in /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/, CI builds it on every push. The plugin header integrations/mumble/include/MumblePlugin.h is Mumble's (from Mumble 1.5.939, BSD-3-Clause, see include/LICENSE.mumble).

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
"waiting for Mumble" although Mumble runs: check that the plugin is enabled in Mumble's settings (Plugins), and that xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin says "In Mumble: ..." with a path. The daemon logs "Voice chat plugin connected (mumble)" when it connects.

Nobody on the strips: the strips show your channel without you; join a channel with other people. People need free auto slots, or person channels on slots (xtouch-daemon check-config shows which slots are auto).

Two Mumble clients at once (e.g. a second one with mumble -m -c <other settings file> to test with another user): enable the plugin in one of them only. The daemon keeps the plugin that connected first and refuses the other one; it logs "Refusing another voice chat plugin while one is connected" once.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Start with the log and the state of the service:

systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon      # is the device, the sound server, the broker connected?
journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f      # the log

For more detail, stop the service and run the daemon in the foreground with xtouch-daemon run -l debug.

items.title: The device
items.text:
The device shows IP: 192.168.001.100 wait.... It is set to its network interface and ignores USB. Switch it to MC mode on USB in its setup menu, see Getting started.

... is it switched on, in MC mode on USB? xtouch-daemon test can't find the sound card of the extender. The daemon waits for it and connects when it appears. Check that it is connected and on, and that /proc/asound/cards lists it. If the name differs, set [device] name to a part of it.

can't open X-Touch-Ext (... Device or resource busy). Only one program can use the device. Stop the daemon before xtouch-daemon test (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon), and close DAWs or other MIDI tools that opened it.

... Permission denied. Your user can't open the MIDI device in /dev/snd. Desktop sessions give access to the logged-in user; without a session, add the user to the audio group. See Hardware.

A fader does not change the volume. Only a touched fader changes a value. A fader whose touch sensor failed goes back to its value after a move. xtouch-daemon test shows whether the device reports fader touched. Until the sensor is repaired, touchless_faders makes the fader work without it.

A fader jumps on its first move after the daemon started. The device can't tell where its faders are, so after a connect the daemon assumes them at the bottom. A fader moved while the daemon did not run jumps from where it really is. See Hardware.

items.title: Audio
items.text:
The meters stay dark. A meter shows a level only while something plays to the output or records from the input. That is on purpose: the meters never open a device themselves. A microphone meter moves only while an application records from it. Check also behavior.meters and the strip's meter.

Streams don't follow when I select another output. Select makes the device the default, and streams without a fixed target follow the default. A stream that another tool moved to a particular device (pavucontrol's per-stream output menu, pactl move-sink-input) stays there. Move it back in pavucontrol, or restart the application's stream.

A strip shows off. The device it controls is not there, e.g. Bluetooth headphones that are switched off. It comes back by itself. xtouch-daemon list-devices shows the devices that are there.

An apps strip shows idle. No stream of its applications is there. xtouch-daemon list-apps shows the names and binaries of the applications that play, and which strip takes each one.

Select does not start the application of launch. The daemon's log says why: a program that is not in PATH (can't launch ...), or one that did not show up in 15 s. Nothing happens either while the strip counts it as running: on apps strips also a process whose name contains a match entry (ps -eo comm shows them). The application's own output is in journalctl --user -u 'xtouch-launch-*'. A graphical application that finds no display there needs the desktop's variables in the systemd user manager (systemctl --user show-environment should list WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY); most desktops import them at login.

An application lands on the wrong strip. xtouch-daemon list-apps names the strip that takes it. An apps strip takes every application whose name or binary contains one of its match entries, so a short entry can match more than intended. check-config shows what the presets in match stand for.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: A change does not show on the device. Reload the daemon after saving: systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon. A file with errors is logged and the old configuration stays: run xtouch-daemon check-config. A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart. The GUI tells whether the device runs the saved file.

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text:
The entities are unavailable. They are available only while the daemon runs and the device is connected. Check the broker settings in [mqtt] and the log. The GUI tells how the connection is doing next to the preview and on the page "Home Assistant", where "Test connection" tries the settings.

A strip shows offline. The broker can't be reached. The daemon connects again by itself.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command What it does xtouch-daemon run Runs the daemon in the foreground. xtouch-daemon check-config Validates the configuration and lists what each strip does. xtouch-daemon init-config Writes the example configuration. xtouch-daemon list-devices Lists outputs, inputs, and the sound cards with their profiles. xtouch-daemon list-apps Lists the applications that play, and which strip takes each one. xtouch-daemon test Tests the LCDs, LEDs, rings, meters and faders, then shows what happens on the device. xtouch-daemon mode Shows the running daemon's mode, or picks another one. xtouch-daemon why Says why a slot shows what it shows, or where a channel is and why. xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin Shows, builds or installs the Mumble plugin of voip strips. xtouch-daemon install-service Sets the daemon up as a systemd user service. xtouch-daemon gui Edits the configuration in a window. xtouch-daemon simulate Prototype: what the slots of a configuration in the format of channels, states and slots show. xtouch-daemon observe Prototype: records what plays, records and runs, for simulate --replay.

Every command takes -h/--help. xtouch-daemon -V (--version) shows the version.

-c FILE (--config FILE) selects the configuration file; the default is ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml.

items.title: run
items.text:
xtouch-daemon run [-c FILE] [-l LEVEL]

Runs the daemon in the foreground. install-service sets it up as a systemd user service instead.

Option Meaning -c, --config FILE The configuration file. -l, --log-level LEVEL debug, info (default), warning or error. debug also logs the messages of the device the daemon doesn't use.

The daemon notes its process and configuration file in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.json while it runs, and serves what the device shows on $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock for the GUI. A second daemon does not start: it names the one that runs.

Signals:

Signal Effect SIGHUP Reloads the configuration (systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon). A file with errors is logged, and the current configuration stays. SIGTERM, SIGINT Stops: the strips go dark from the right and the faders go down.

items.title: check-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon check-config [-c FILE]

Validates the configuration, describes each channel and shows a table of what the slots show in which states. Without a file at the default path it checks the defaults. Example output:

/home/me/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml: valid
Channels:
  out: 'Speaker' output alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo, select makes it the default (cyan, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: balance)
  mic: the default input (red, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: balance)
  browser: 'Browser' applications @browsers (firefox, chromium, ...) (yellow, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: media)
  lamp: 'Living' Home Assistant, entities *.*_lamp_* (yellow)
What the slots show:
when     1    2        3     4-8
default  out  browser  auto  auto
call     out  browser  mic   auto

A channel with choices lists them, e.g. output: Phones, Speaker or Buds (Select switches). A channel whose meter shows the level after its fader (meter_point = "post_fader", see Meters) says meter post-fader.

A file with errors names the place of each one, e.g. channel.mic.label: String should have at most 7 characters, and the command fails. The command lists the channels and shows the table of what the slots show in which states.

items.title: init-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon init-config [PATH] [-f]

Writes the example configuration with channels, states and slots to ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml, or to PATH. An existing file stays, unless -f (--force) overwrites it.

items.title: list-devices
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-devices

Lists the outputs and inputs with the node names to use as device, their descriptions, volumes and states; * marks the defaults. Then it lists each sound card by its name and description, with its devices and its profiles (name and description), for card and profile of choices and for profiles; * marks the active ones:

Profiles of alsa_card.pci-0000_11_00.4, Family 17h/19h HD Audio Controller (alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo):
  * output:analog-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Analog Stereo Output + Analog Stereo Input
    output:iec958-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Digital Stereo (IEC958) Output + Analog Stereo Input

items.title: list-apps
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-apps [-c FILE]

Lists the applications that play now: their names (and aliases), the presets they are part of (e.g. Brave (@browsers)), binaries and volumes, and which strip takes each one: an apps strip, an auto strip, "ignored" (behavior.ignore) or no strip. Use the names and binaries, or the presets, for match, ignore and [aliases].

items.title: test
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test [-c FILE] [--no-events]

Lights up everything on the device and moves the faders: every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader up and down. Then it shows what you do on the device (faders, touches, buttons, encoders), and the messages from the device the daemon doesn't use, until Ctrl+C. --no-events ends after the test.

It takes the name of the device from [device] of the configuration. Stop the daemon first (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon): only one program can use the device.

items.title: virtual-device
items.text:
xtouch-daemon virtual-device [--broken-touch 1,4] [--log-level debug]

A virtual X-Touch Extender, for trying the daemon without the device: xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device (or [device] virtual = true) drives it instead of the real one, and the GUI shows what it shows. It runs headless until interrupted (Ctrl+C); the GUI can host one itself, with the mouse on its strips. One daemon at a time can use it.

Option Meaning --broken-touch The faders (from 1) whose touch sensor failed: they never report a touch, see Motor faders. --log-level debug also logs every message of the daemon.

items.title: mode
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mode [NAME | auto | --next | --previous]

Without arguments it prints the modes of the running daemon, marks the one that is on, and says whether it was picked by hand. mode gaming picks the mode gaming, --next and --previous the one after or before it, auto lets the rules decide again. It talks to the daemon over its live view socket, so it needs a running daemon.

items.title: why
items.text:
